title: A Centurion's Faith, a Widow's Son, and a Forgiven Woman
summary: Jesus heals the servant of a Gentile centurion whose faith surpasses anything he has found in Israel, and at Nain he raises a widow's only son. From prison John the Baptist sends to ask whether Jesus is the one to come; Jesus points to his works and honors John as more than a prophet. At a Pharisee's dinner a sinful woman anoints his feet, and Jesus tells a parable of two debtors to show why the forgiven love much.
story:
The Sermon on the Plain (6:20-49) described the kingdom's way of life. This chapter shows who actually receives the kingdom, and the answer keeps surprising: a Roman-style officer who is not a Jew, a grieving widow, tax collectors who accepted John's baptism, and a woman known in town as a sinner. Meanwhile, the respectable reject God's purpose for themselves (verse 30). At Nazareth Jesus had said that Elijah was sent to a widow of Sidon and Elisha cleansed a Syrian (4:25-27), and the townspeople tried to kill him for it. Now the pattern he described begins to happen before the reader's eyes.

Luke also settles an important question at this stage. John had announced a coming one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire and burn the chaff (3:16-17), and Jesus' ministry of healing and table fellowship is not what everyone expected. The chapter's middle section lets John ask the question aloud, and Jesus answers with Isaiah's own descriptions of the age of salvation. The chapter ends with the question the whole Gospel is building toward: “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (verse 49). Chapter 8 will open with the women who traveled with Jesus, some of them healed and forgiven, and move on to the parable of the sower, which explains why the same word produces such different responses.
historical:
A centurion (hekatontarchos, the Greek for the Latin centurio) commanded a century, nominally a hundred men and in practice about eighty. Capernaum lay in Galilee, which was ruled from 4 BC to AD 39 by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, not by a Roman governor, and no Roman legion was stationed in Galilee before the region came under direct Roman rule in AD 44. So this officer was most likely in Antipas's service, in a force organized on Roman lines and often recruited from non-Jews in the region; Josephus describes Antipas's army being destroyed by the Nabatean king Aretas IV around AD 36 (Antiquities 18.113-115). Some Gentiles in this period admired Judaism, attended synagogues, and gave money for them without becoming full converts. Luke calls such people God-fearers in Acts (10:2, 13:16, 13:26), and the Roman centurion Cornelius at Caesarea is his fullest example. The elders' plea that this man loves the nation and built the synagogue (verse 5) fits that pattern exactly. The synagogue now seen at Capernaum is a white limestone building of the late fourth or fifth century AD, but the Franciscan excavators Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda (1969 onward) found basalt foundations and a cobbled floor beneath it; Corbo took them to be the first-century synagogue, while Loffreda thought they belonged to an intermediate stage, so the link to this verse is possible but not proven.

Matthew 8:5-13 tells the same healing more briefly, with the centurion speaking to Jesus in person. Luke has him send first Jewish elders and then friends, so that he never meets Jesus at all. Ancient readers were used to a principal's words and acts being reported as his own when carried by agents, and many commentators explain the difference that way; others think Luke has preserved the fuller form of the story and Matthew compressed it. John 4:46-54 tells a similar healing at a distance for a royal official at Capernaum, and interpreters differ on whether it is the same event. A Jewish parallel is instructive: the Babylonian Talmud (b. Berakhot 34b) tells how the Galilean holy man Hanina ben Dosa, a first-century figure, prayed for the sick son of Rabban Gamaliel and told the messengers that the fever had left him, and they later found it had left at that very hour. Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) used such stories to place Jesus among Galilean charismatic holy men. The comparison shows that healing at a distance was not unthinkable to Jewish hearers; Luke's account differs in that Jesus speaks no prayer and simply exercises authority.

Nain was a village in lower Galilee, usually identified with the modern Arab village of Nein on the northern slope of the Hill of Moreh, about six miles south-southeast of Nazareth. On the other side of the same hill lay Shunem, where Elisha raised the Shunammite woman's son (2 Kings 4:8-37), and Elijah had raised the son of a widow at Zarephath near Sidon (1 Kings 17:17-24). Luke alone records the raising at Nain.

John, meanwhile, was in prison under Antipas (3:19-20). Josephus places his imprisonment and execution at Machaerus, Herod's fortress east of the Dead Sea, and says Antipas feared John's influence over the crowds might lead to revolt (Antiquities 18.116-119). Matthew 11:2-19 records the same exchange with John's disciples. John's question and Jesus' answer have a striking parallel among the Dead Sea Scrolls. A fragment from Cave 4 at Qumran, 4Q521 (sometimes called the Messianic Apocalypse), copied around the first century BC, says that in the coming day the Lord will heal the wounded, give life to the dead, and proclaim good news to the poor, in a passage that also speaks of heaven and earth listening to his anointed one. Its list overlaps with Jesus' reply in verse 22, including the raising of the dead, which Isaiah 61 does not mention. It shows that some Jews of the period expected exactly these works when God's anointed age arrived.
cultural:
A widow who lost her only son lost her protector, her advocate, and very likely her means of support in a society where women seldom owned land or earned wages; Scripture repeatedly names widows, orphans, and strangers as those God himself defends (Exodus 22:22-24, Deuteronomy 10:18). Burial took place quickly, usually on the day of death, outside the town, and the body was carried on an open bier (soros in verse 14, a word that can mean a coffin but here must be a litter, since the young man sits up). Mourning was loud and public. A later rule in the Mishnah, attributed to Rabbi Judah, says that even the poorest man in Israel should provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (m. Ketubbot 4:4), and the large crowd with the widow (verse 12) shows a town turning out to share her grief. Contact with a corpse made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11-16), and later rabbinic law extended impurity to what carried the body. Jesus touches the bier; Luke does not comment on impurity, but the gesture puts his life-giving power where death was.

At formal dinners guests reclined on couches or cushions, leaning on the left elbow with their feet stretched out behind them, away from the table. That is how the woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet (verse 38). A meal in a notable person's house was semi-public: doors could be open, and people who were not guests might come in to watch and listen. Ordinary hospitality offered water for guests' dusty feet (Genesis 18:4, Judges 19:21), a kiss of greeting, and sometimes oil for the head (Psalm 23:5); Simon gave none of these, and though they were courtesies rather than strict obligations, their absence was noticeable. The woman supplies all three, and more lavishly than any host would: tears for water, kisses on the feet rather than the cheek, perfume rather than olive oil.

Her letting down her hair would have been striking. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, lists a wife's going out in public with her head uncovered among the breaches of Jewish custom for which a husband could divorce her without paying her marriage settlement (m. Ketubbot 7:6), and Numbers 5:18 has the priest loosen the hair of a woman suspected of adultery. The rule is later than Luke and reflects rabbinic circles, but it suggests how the gesture would look to a Pharisee's guests. Luke calls her “a sinful woman from that town” (verse 37) but does not say what her sin was. The long tradition that she was a prostitute is an inference from her reputation and her hair; the text itself never says so. Alabaster (alabastron) was a soft translucent stone used for small sealed flasks of perfume, and perfumed oil (muron) was costly. A denarius was roughly a day's wage for a laborer (Matthew 20:2), so the two debts in the parable are about a year and a half's wages and about two months' wages.

Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law, including purity and tithing, and to the traditions of the elders; Josephus (Antiquities 18.12-15) says they were respected by the people. Simon's invitation is not hostile, and he calls Jesus Teacher (verse 40). His private thought (verse 39) turns on a common assumption: a true prophet would know who was touching him and would keep his distance from a sinner.
literary:
The chapter builds carefully toward the question of verse 49. Its two opening miracles mirror the Elijah and Elisha stories Jesus cited at Nazareth (4:25-27): a Gentile benefits from Israel's prophet, and a widow's son is raised and, in words that repeat the Greek Old Testament of 1 Kings 17:23 almost exactly, Jesus “gave him back to his mother” (verse 15). The crowd draws the natural conclusion, “A great prophet has appeared among us!” (verse 16), and adds, “God has visited His people!”, echoing Zechariah's song (1:68, 1:78). The chapter then asks whether prophet is a big enough word. John is more than a prophet (verse 26); Jesus is the one who fulfills what Isaiah said God would do, and the one who forgives sins.

Jesus' reply to John (verse 22) is a mosaic of Isaiah: the blind see and the deaf hear (Isaiah 29:18, 35:5), the lame walk (35:6), the dead are raised (26:19), and good news is preached to the poor (61:1, the text Jesus read at Nazareth in 4:18). Only the cleansing of lepers has no clear Isaianic source, and it recalls Elisha and Naaman (4:27). In verse 27 Jesus quotes a blend of Malachi 3:1 and Exodus 23:20 to identify John as the messenger who prepares the way.

The centurion's story is built on a contrast of worthiness. The elders say he is worthy (axios, verse 4); he says he is not worthy (ou hikanos, verse 6; ouk axioō, verse 7). The chapter's closing scene makes a similar contrast between Simon, who judges the woman, and the woman, whom Jesus defends. The children's game in verses 31-35, in which one group pipes a wedding tune or sings a funeral dirge and the other refuses to join either, is a parable of a generation that finds fault with every messenger: John was too austere, Jesus too convivial. The insult glutton and drunkard (verse 34) echoes the charge against the rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20, a charge that carried the death penalty.

The dinner scene (36-50) contains a parable inside a story. Jesus answers Simon's unspoken thought (proving himself the prophet Simon doubted), tells a two-line parable, gets Simon to pass judgment on himself (verse 43), and then turns to the woman while still speaking to Simon, contrasting his hospitality with hers in three balanced pairs (verses 44-46: water, kiss, oil). The scene closes with two pronouncements to the woman, “Your sins are forgiven” (verse 48) and “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (verse 50), with the guests' question between them. Luke also frames the chapter with love: the centurion “loves our nation” (verse 5), and the woman “has loved much” (verse 47).

outline.t: The widow's son raised at Nain
A sinful woman anoints Jesus at Simon's table

doctrines.note: John asks whether Jesus is “the One who was to come” (verse 19), and Jesus answers not with a title but with the works Isaiah and later Jewish hope assigned to God's anointed age (verse 22). He is the Messiah, but not the one some expected: the judgment John announced is real, and its first form is mercy to the blind, the poor, and the dead.

The centurion trusts that Jesus' word has authority at a distance, as a commander's word does, and Jesus calls it greater faith than he has found in Israel (verse 9). The woman's faith saves her (verse 50). In both cases faith is humble reliance on Jesus rather than a claim of worthiness.

Luke uses the verb dikaioō twice: the people and tax collectors “acknowledged God’s justice” (literally, justified God) by accepting John's baptism (verse 29), and wisdom is vindicated, or justified, by her children (verse 35). The dinner scene then shows what that verdict looks like for a sinner: her sins are forgiven, she is declared saved by faith, and her love is the evidence of that forgiveness, not its price (verse 47).

The parable of the two debtors teaches that love for God grows from the experience of being forgiven: the one forgiven more loves more (verses 42-43). The woman's extravagant love and Simon's cool correctness are both explained by how each understands their debt.

The raising of the widow's son is a return to mortal life rather than the resurrection to glory, since the young man would die again. But it is a sign of the power that will raise the dead, and Jesus lists “the dead are raised” among the marks of the age of salvation (verse 22).

words.note: Splagchnizomai, to have compassion, to be moved in one's inner parts. The related noun splagchna means the inward organs, where ancient people located deep feeling. The verb occurs 12 times in the New Testament, all in the Synoptic Gospels, and three times in Luke: here, of the Samaritan (10:33), and of the father of the lost son (15:20). In the Gospels it is used only of Jesus or of figures in his parables who act as God acts. At Nain it comes before any request: no one asks Jesus for help.

Episkeptomai, to visit, look after, care for. It occurs 11 times in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it often describes God coming to his people to rescue them (Genesis 50:24, Exodus 4:31) or to judge. Luke uses it three times in the sense of God's saving visit: twice in Zechariah's song (1:68, 1:78) and here in the crowd's cry, “God has visited His people!” (verse 16). The raising at Nain is read as the fulfillment of that song.

Dikaioō, to justify, declare or show to be in the right. It occurs 39 times in the New Testament, 15 of them in Romans, and five in Luke. Standard lexicons (BDAG) give senses ranging from render a favorable verdict to vindicate. In verse 29 people justify God, which cannot mean make him righteous: they acknowledge that God is in the right by accepting his messenger. In verse 35 wisdom is vindicated by her children, shown right by the lives she produces. The word describes a verdict, not a process of moral improvement, which is how Paul will use it too.

Aphiēmi, to let go, release, leave, permit, and so to forgive, remit a debt. It occurs 143 times in the New Testament and 31 times in Luke, most often in senses other than forgiveness. The parable shows why the word suits forgiveness: a debt is released (verse 42 uses the synonym charizomai, to cancel as a favor). In verse 47 the perfect passive, apheōntai, her sins have been forgiven and stand forgiven, describes a state already true before Jesus announces it in verse 48.

Agapaō, to love. It occurs 143 times in the New Testament, 13 of them in Luke, and five times in this chapter. It frames the chapter: the centurion loves the nation (verse 5), and the woman loved much (verse 47). In the parable (verse 42) Jesus asks which debtor will love the lender more, making love the grateful response of the forgiven. The verb is not in itself a special divine love as distinct from other loves, as older word studies claimed; its meaning comes from its object and its context.

Hamartōlos, sinner, sinful. It occurs 47 times in the New Testament, and 18 of them are in Luke, more than in any other book. In the Gospels it often labels people whose way of life or occupation put them outside respectable piety, such as tax collectors (verse 34). Luke uses it of the woman twice (verses 37 and 39) and never softens it, but he shows Jesus receiving such people as the physician receives the sick (5:31-32, 15:1-2).

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal, make whole. It occurs 106 times in the New Testament, 17 of them in Luke. Luke uses it both for physical healing (8:48, 17:19, 18:42, where the same sentence, Your faith has saved you, means your faith has healed you) and for rescue from sin and its consequences (19:10). In verse 50 no physical illness is in view: the woman is forgiven, accepted, and sent in peace, which in the Hebrew sense of shalom means wholeness restored. Verse 3 uses the compound diasōzō for the servant's healing.

christ:
This chapter answers John's question from many sides. Jesus is the one whose word heals at a distance, as a commander's word is obeyed (verses 7-8), and whose touch stops a funeral procession and reverses death. He acts with a compassion that goes to the grieving widow before anyone asks (verse 13). Luke calls him the Lord in verse 13, the first time the narrator himself uses that title of Jesus in the story of his ministry, and the crowd's cry that God has visited his people (verse 16) turns Zechariah's hope (1:68) into an event. Like Elijah he gives a son back to his mother, but Elijah stretched himself on the child three times and cried to the Lord (1 Kings 17:21), while Jesus simply speaks to the dead man: “I tell you, get up!”

He is more than the great prophet the crowd sees. His answer to John fulfills what Isaiah said would happen when God himself comes to save (Isaiah 35:4-6), and he forgives sins on his own authority, which the guests rightly recognize as the prerogative of God (verse 49; compare 5:21). Jesus also claims that John, the greatest of those born of women, is the messenger who prepares the way before the Lord (verse 27, Malachi 3:1). If John prepares the way of the Lord, Jesus is the Lord whose way he prepares.

The chapter also shows what kind of Messiah he is. He is accused of being a friend of tax collectors and sinners (verse 34), and Luke's story shows the charge to be true in a way the accusers did not intend. His answer to John contains a gentle warning, “Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me” (verse 23): Jesus is not always the Messiah people expect, and blessing belongs to those who trust him anyway. His defense of the woman anticipates the purpose Luke will state outright: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (19:10). The one who receives her tears will himself be anointed for burial and give his life for sinners; the debt the parable describes as simply cancelled is one the Gospel will show him paying.
interpretation:
Augustine (Sermon 62) held up the centurion as the model of humility that makes room for Christ: by counting himself unworthy to receive Christ under his roof, he received him into his heart. The centurion's words entered the liturgy. In the Roman Mass, from the medieval period, the people say before communion, in words adapted from Matthew 8:8 and Luke 7:6-7, that they are not worthy that the Lord should come under their roof, but only say the word and their soul shall be healed. Ambrose of Milan, in his Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke (around 389), read the widow of Nain as a figure of the church, mourning her children dead in sin and receiving them back alive.

John's question divided early interpreters. Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.18, around 208) held that John genuinely stumbled, because the prophetic Spirit that had rested on him had passed to Christ, leaving John an ordinary man. John Chrysostom (Homily 36 on Matthew, around 390) argued the opposite: John did not doubt but sent his disciples so that they, and the crowds, would be convinced by seeing Jesus' works for themselves. Most modern commentators take the question as real puzzlement from a prophet whose expectations of judgment were not being met in the way he had pictured.

The anointing scene has the richest and most tangled history. All four Gospels tell of a woman anointing Jesus: Luke here, in Galilee, early, in the house of Simon the Pharisee; Mark 14:3-9 and Matthew 26:6-13 at Bethany in the last week, in the house of Simon the leper, where an unnamed woman pours nard on his head; and John 12:1-8, at Bethany six days before Passover, where Mary the sister of Martha anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair. Most commentators, including Raymond Brown (The Gospel according to John I-XII, 1966), distinguish two events, a Galilean anointing by a penitent (Luke) and a Bethany anointing before the passion (Mark, Matthew, John), and think details crossed between the stories as they were retold; John's scene of Mary wiping perfume off with her hair reads most naturally as influenced by Luke's tears. Luke, notably, omits the Bethany anointing from his passion narrative.

In the West the women were gradually merged. Pope Gregory the Great, in a homily on this passage probably preached in 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 33), identified Luke's sinful woman with Mary of Bethany and with Mary Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out (8:2), and read the seven demons as all the vices. The homily was preaching, not a doctrinal decree, but it shaped Western devotion for a millennium; Mary Magdalene became the penitent of Latin art, and the Roman Mass for her feast on July 22 read this passage. The Eastern churches never made the identification. They honor Mary Magdalene as a myrrh-bearer and equal to the apostles, and commemorate the women separately. In 1517 the French humanist Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples argued in a treatise on Mary Magdalene that the three were distinct women, and the theology faculty of Paris (the Sorbonne) condemned that view in 1521. The Roman Catholic Church revised its calendar in 1969: the memorial of July 22 was kept for Mary Magdalene alone, the Gospel reading from Luke 7 was replaced with John 20:1-2, 11-18, her meeting with the risen Christ, and the calendar's commentary separated her from Mary of Bethany and the woman of Luke 7. In 2016 a decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship, at Pope Francis's wish, raised her memorial to a feast with a preface calling her apostle of the apostles, a title with roots in Hippolytus of Rome's early third-century Commentary on the Song of Songs, where the women who carried the Easter news are called apostles sent to the apostles, and later in Thomas Aquinas.

The Reformation argued over verse 47. Readers who took the woman's love as the ground of her forgiveness found in it support for forgiveness through contrition joined with charity; John Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555), insisted from the parable itself that her love was the sign and fruit of a forgiveness already received, and most modern commentators, Catholic and Protestant, read the grammar the same way. Søren Kierkegaard wrote on the woman in his Three Discourses at the Communion on Fridays (1849), treating her silent love as an image of faith. In art, Dieric Bouts painted Christ in the House of Simon (about 1445 to 1460, now in Berlin), Peter Paul Rubens painted The Feast in the House of Simon the Pharisee (about 1618 to 1620, now in the Hermitage). In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C, the chapter is read on consecutive Sundays after Pentecost (7:1-10, 7:11-17, and 7:36-8:3), and the Roman lectionary reads 7:11-17 and 7:36-8:3 on the tenth and eleventh Sundays in Ordinary Time in Year C. The Jewish scholar Amy-Jill Levine, writing with Ben Witherington III (The Gospel of Luke, 2018), warns against making Simon a stock villain; he hosts Jesus and judges the parable rightly.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the Greek manuscripts. In verse 11 the text most editors print reads en tō hexēs, ‘soon afterward’, while other manuscripts read en tē hexēs, ‘on the next day’, which the King James Version follows (‘the day after’). In verse 19 the critical text has John send to ‘the Lord’, while the later Byzantine manuscripts behind the King James Version have ‘Jesus’. In verse 28 the Textus Receptus adds ‘prophet’, so the King James Version reads that there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist; most manuscripts and modern versions read simply that no one born of women is greater than John. In verse 31 the King James Version begins, ‘And the Lord said’, a phrase found in late manuscripts and absent from the earliest, which modern versions omit. None of these changes the sense of the passage.

Verse 35 differs between the Gospels rather than the manuscripts: Luke has wisdom vindicated by all her children, while Matthew 11:19 has ‘by her actions’ (her works), and some manuscripts of each Gospel have been assimilated to the other. In verse 47 translations handle the conjunction hoti differently. The King James Version and some modern versions read ‘her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much’, which can sound as if her love earned forgiveness. The conjunction can give the ground of a statement (I say this because) as well as the cause of an event, and the parable (verses 41-43) and the second half of the verse (the one forgiven little loves little) show that her love is the evidence of forgiveness, which is why the BSB and several other modern versions render it ‘because her many sins have been forgiven, she has loved much’.

teach.big: Jesus is the Lord who comes with God's saving power to the unworthy, and those who know how much they have been forgiven respond with faith and extravagant love.

outline.t: Faith is not a claim of worthiness but trust in the authority of Jesus' word; an outsider can show more of it than the insiders.
Jesus' compassion goes first to the grieving before anyone asks, and his word is stronger than death: God has visited his people.
When Jesus does not act as we expected, he answers with what he is actually doing, and blesses those who do not stumble over him.
John is the greatest of the old era, yet the least in the kingdom stands in a greater privilege; how people received John's call exposed how they stood with God.
A generation that rejects both the austere prophet and the feasting Messiah is not looking for truth but for reasons; wisdom is proved right by the lives it changes.
Love for Jesus grows out of knowing we have been forgiven much; the self-righteous miss both their debt and the Savior at their own table.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first makes verse 47 teach that the woman earned forgiveness by loving much. The parable and the second half of the verse run the other way: love follows forgiveness, and verse 50 grounds her salvation in faith. The second identifies her with Mary Magdalene and preaches her as a reformed prostitute. Luke names neither her sin nor her, and Mary Magdalene is introduced as a new character in 8:2; the identification is a later Western tradition that the Roman Catholic Church itself set aside in 1969. The third turns Simon into a cartoon Pharisee. He invited Jesus, called him Teacher, and answered the parable correctly; the text's challenge is sharper if the listener recognizes in Simon a decent religious person who cannot see his own need.

With the centurion, avoid treating him as a lesson in positive thinking, as if faith were confidence that one's request will be granted. His faith rests on Jesus' authority and is expressed in humility. With John's question, avoid either scolding John for weak faith or denying that he doubted; Jesus does neither, and immediately honors him. With the children in the marketplace, avoid the moral that the church should simply be more attractive; Jesus' point is that some refusals have nothing to do with style. Finally, do not use the raising at Nain to promise that faith will always prevent or reverse a death. Luke presents it as a sign of the kingdom's arrival, and the young man would die again.
teach.pastoral: The Nain story will press on anyone in the room who has buried a child or walked behind a coffin, especially widows and parents. Let Jesus' compassion be the point: he sees the mother first and speaks to her grief. Avoid implying that those whose dead were not raised lacked faith; the woman at Nain did not ask for anything. The dinner scene will press on those who carry shame, whether for sexual sin, for being the subject of gossip, or for abuse they suffered and wrongly blame themselves for. Speak of her as Luke does, without speculation about her past, and let Jesus' public defense of her be heard. It will also touch people scrupulous about forgiveness, who fear their love for God is too small to count. The text answers that love is the fruit of forgiveness received, not the price of it, so the remedy for weak love is to look again at the size of the debt that has been cancelled. John's question in prison speaks to believers who are suffering and doubting at once: Jesus did not rebuke him and called him great.

hard.q: Why would John the Baptist, who baptized Jesus and saw the Spirit descend on him, doubt whether he was the one?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real. Luke has told the reader that John leaped in the womb at Mary's greeting (1:41) and that he announced a mightier one to come (3:16), and the other Gospels have him recognize Jesus at the baptism (Matthew 3:14, John 1:29-34). Some historical critics take the question as evidence that John never recognized Jesus as Messiah at all and that Christian tradition later made him a witness; on this view the scenes of recognition are the church's addition and the question from prison is the older memory. Jewish readers have sometimes seen the exchange the same way, as a trace of rivalry between the followers of John and of Jesus (compare Acts 19:1-7, where disciples of John are still found in Ephesus).

Christian interpreters have answered in three main ways. John Chrysostom (Homily 36 on Matthew) and many after him argued that John himself did not doubt but sent his disciples so that they would see Jesus' works and transfer their loyalty. That reading protects John's steadfastness but struggles with Luke's wording, since John himself frames the question and Jesus replies, Go back and report to John. Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.18) held that John did doubt, because the prophetic Spirit had passed from him to Christ. Most modern commentators take the question as genuine puzzlement rather than unbelief: John had announced a coming one with an axe at the root of the trees and a winnowing fork in his hand, who would burn the chaff (3:9, 3:17), and he now sat in Herod's prison while Jesus healed, ate with sinners, and brought no judgment on the wicked. A prophet can be certain of his calling and still perplexed about how God is fulfilling it. Against the skeptical reading, these interpreters note that an early church eager to make John a witness would hardly have invented a scene that makes him look uncertain, which is itself an argument that the scene is old. Jesus neither rebukes John nor gives a simple yes; he points to deeds that match Isaiah's promises and then praises him publicly. The answer suggests that judgment is real, but that the Messiah's first coming is marked by mercy, with the harvest still to come.

hard.q: Is the sinful woman of Luke 7 the same person as Mary Magdalene or Mary of Bethany?
hard.a:
The case for identification has a long pedigree and is stronger than it first appears. All four Gospels tell of a woman anointing Jesus; Luke's woman and John's Mary both anoint his feet and wipe them with their hair (7:38, John 12:3), an unusual shared detail; Luke's host is named Simon, as is the host at Bethany in Mark 14:3; and Mary Magdalene is introduced immediately afterward (8:2). Gregory the Great (Homily 33, around 591) drew these threads together and identified all three women, and the identification governed Western preaching, art, and liturgy until modern times. Some Catholic writers still defend a version of it, arguing that the tradition preserves a memory the Gospels do not spell out.

The responses are several. The settings differ: Luke's scene is in Galilee, early in the ministry, in a Pharisee's house, and turns on forgiveness; the Bethany scene is in Judea, six days before Passover, in the house of Simon the leper or of Lazarus's family, and turns on burial. Simon was one of the most common Jewish names of the period. Luke introduces Mary Magdalene in 8:2 as a new character, with no hint that the reader has just met her, and describes her as healed of demons, which Luke never equates with sexual sin. Mary of Bethany appears in Luke 10:38-42 as someone Luke's readers have not met either. The Eastern churches never accepted the identification; the Reformer-era humanist Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples argued against it in 1517; and in 1969 the Roman Catholic calendar distinguished Mary Magdalene from the other two. Most modern commentators across traditions, Raymond Brown among them, treat them as three women. What is not in dispute is that nothing in Scripture calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute; that portrait belongs to later tradition, and it has often obscured her role in the Gospels as a follower of Jesus from Galilee and the first witness of his resurrection.
